stem: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the application on an instance stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks
stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the results of the target group health checks.
options.why: For an instance that fails the target group check, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and the group [replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced), with one setting and no code.

options.text: Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.
options.why: By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, and the running instance passes its EC2 status checks, so it stays in service.

options.text: Run a script on each instance that tests the application every minute and calls the Auto Scaling API to mark the instance unhealthy when a test fails.
options.why: It works, because a custom check can [mark that particular instance as](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-custom-health-check-immediate-replace) unhealthy, but the team writes code that one setting replaces.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group waits longer before it checks the health of each new instance.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new instance for failed health; it adds no load balancer check.
options.misconception: believes the grace period decides which health checks the group uses

explanation: The application fails while the instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks the instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced).
takeaway: A running instance with a failed application needs the ELB health check type on the group.
twin: If the stem said "the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check" instead: keep the current settings, because EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default).
say: The group ignores the load balancer checks until you turn them on, so I'd set the health check type to ELB.

stem: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks
fails its EC2 system status check

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the results of the target group health checks.
options.why: It works, but it is a change that this failure does not need, because the EC2 status checks of the group already catch impaired hardware.

options.text: Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.
options.why: EC2 status checks are [always enabled](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-ec2-status-checks-always-enabled) for the group, and an instance whose [hardware has become impaired](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-unhealthy-instance-definition) counts as unhealthy and is replaced.

options.text: Run a script on each instance that tests the application every minute and calls the Auto Scaling API to mark the instance unhealthy when a test fails.
options.why: It adds code to maintain, and a script on failed hardware stops with the hardware; the default EC2 checks already find this failure.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group waits longer before it checks the health of each new instance.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new instance for failed health; it changes no check.
options.misconception: believes the grace period decides which health checks the group uses

explanation: The hardware fails, so the instance fails its EC2 system status check. EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default) of the group, and the group [automatically terminates it and replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-replaces-impaired-instance). The current settings meet the requirement with no change and no work.
takeaway: Impaired hardware fails the EC2 status checks, and the group acts on those checks with its default settings.
twin: If the stem said "the application on an instance stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running" instead: turn on ELB health checks, because the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) checks by default.
say: The EC2 status checks are on in every group, so a hardware failure is already replaced; no change needed.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon ECS. The application stores orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table that uses provisioned capacity mode. During sales events, the number of requests grows quickly and then falls again. The company wants the number of ECS tasks and the read and write capacity of the table to follow the load automatically. Which AWS service should a solutions architect use to scale both resources?
keywords: read and write capacity of the table

options.text: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, with an Auto Scaling group whose scaling policy adds ECS tasks and DynamoDB table capacity
options.why: EC2 Auto Scaling is the choice when you [only need to scale Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-use-ec2-vs-aws-auto-scaling) groups; tasks and table capacity are not instances in a group.

options.text: Application Auto Scaling, with a target tracking scaling policy for the ECS service and another one for the DynamoDB table
options.why: Application Auto Scaling scales resources other than EC2 instances, and it supports [target tracking scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-policy-types) for the ECS service and for the table.

options.text: Elastic Load Balancing, with an Application Load Balancer that spreads the growing number of requests across the ECS tasks
options.why: A load balancer [automatically distributes your incoming traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-what-distributes-traffic-across-targets) across targets, but it adds no tasks and no table capacity.
options.misconception: believes that spreading requests adds capacity

options.text: Amazon CloudFront, with a distribution that caches the responses of the ECS tasks so that fewer requests reach the table
options.why: A cache in front of the tasks changes neither the number of ECS tasks nor the read and write capacity of the table.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in front of an application scales its resources

explanation: An ECS service and a DynamoDB table are not EC2 instances. For resources like these, [you can use the Application Auto Scaling API](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-faq-application-auto-scaling-for-non-ec2). An ECS service supports [auto scaling of its task count](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-scalable-dimension-examples), and a table in provisioned mode scales [the read and write capacity of the table](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-scalable-dimension-examples).
takeaway: EC2 instances scale with EC2 Auto Scaling; ECS tasks and DynamoDB capacity scale with Application Auto Scaling.
twin: If the stem said "a fleet of EC2 instances" instead: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, because for instances you [use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-wa-ec2-auto-scaling-for-instances-application-auto-scaling-for-other-services).
say: ECS tasks and DynamoDB capacity aren't EC2, so I'd use Application Auto Scaling for both.

stem: A company runs stateless video-encoding workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The workers take jobs from a queue, and the jobs can tolerate interruption and can be restarted, but each restart delays a job, so Spot interruptions must stay rare. At least two workers must keep running even if Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity. The number of other workers changes with the number of jobs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: At least two workers must keep running

options.text: Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 2 instances, and use Spot Instances for all capacity above the base.
options.why: Anything above the base can run on Spot, or on a [specified percentage mix of On-Demand or Spot instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above); here the mix is all Spot.

options.text: Run every worker as an On-Demand Instance, and scale the group with a target tracking policy on the backlog per instance.
options.why: It works, but Spot Instances cost [up to 90%](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-discount-up-to-90-percent) less than On-Demand prices, and these jobs can be restarted.

options.text: Specify one instance type in the mixed instances policy, and use the lowest-price allocation strategy for the Spot Instances.
options.why: The lowest-price strategy has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-lowest-price-not-recommended), and one instance type gives Spot fewer pools to choose from.

options.text: Specify several instance types in the mixed instances policy, and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy for the Spot Instances.
options.why: Several instance types give Spot more pools, and this strategy picks pools that are [least likely to be interrupted](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended) at a low price.

options.text: Run every worker as a Spot Instance, and turn on instance scale-in protection so that Amazon EC2 does not reclaim two of the workers.
options.why: Spot interruptions [bypass all Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling protection mechanisms](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection), so scale-in protection keeps no worker running.

explanation: AWS lets the [base capacity be fulfilled with On-Demand instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above), so two workers stay out of Spot, and the rest runs on Spot. For Spot, be [flexible about which instance types you request](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-be-flexible-types-and-azs), and use the [price and capacity optimized allocation strategy](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended) that AWS recommends.
takeaway: Keep the required minimum on an On-Demand base, run the rest on Spot, and diversify the instance types.
twin: If the stem said "the jobs cannot be restarted" instead: On-Demand Instances, because Spot does not suit work that is [inflexible, stateful, fault-intolerant, or tightly coupled](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-not-suitable-stateful-inflexible).
say: An On-Demand base of two, Spot above it, and several instance types with price-capacity-optimized.

stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Traffic follows a predictable daily pattern with a peak every morning; after the peak, the load falls to a level that changes from day to day. The group has one predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode and no other scaling policy. The instances are ready before each morning peak, but the group keeps its peak capacity for the rest of the day and through the night, and the monthly cost has grown. The application must stay ready for the morning peak. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: keeps its peak capacity for the rest of the day

options.text: Switch the predictive scaling policy to forecast only mode, so that the policy removes the extra instances when the forecast falls.
options.why: In [forecast only](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-forecast-only-mode-first) mode the policy forecasts capacity but does not scale the group, so it removes nothing and also stops the morning scale-out.

options.text: Add a scheduled action each evening that sets the desired capacity to the night level, and keep the predictive scaling policy.
options.why: It works, but capacity stays at the peak level until the evening, and a fixed night level cannot follow a load that changes each day.

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and keep the predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode.
options.why: Target tracking removes instances when the metric falls below the target, and the predictive policy keeps [launching capacity in advance of forecasted load](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-long-initialization-fit).

options.text: Let predictive scaling raise and lower the maximum capacity of the group automatically when the forecast changes.
options.why: A maximum that predictive scaling raised [does not automatically decrease back](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-raised-max-stays) to the original value, so this setting cannot lower it.
options.misconception: believes that predictive scaling lowers the maximum capacity again after it raised it

explanation: Predictive scaling adds instances ahead of the forecast, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in). You can [combine predictive scaling and dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-combine-policy-types-predictive-plus-dynamic): the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready, and the target tracking policy removes instances when the load falls.
takeaway: Pair predictive scaling with target tracking: predictive scaling adds capacity early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in).
twin: If the stem said "traffic has no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking without the predictive policy, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
say: Predictive scaling only scales out, so I'd add target tracking to bring capacity down at night.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that is MOST cost-effective.
I mark the constraints: one predictive policy in forecast and scale mode, the mornings must stay ready, and capacity stays at the peak level for the rest of the day and through the night.
Before I look at the options, I predict forecast only mode, because I think that mode lets the forecast remove the extra instances at night.
I remove the option that raises and lowers the maximum automatically, because a maximum that predictive scaling raised does not go back down automatically.

Between forecast only mode and a target tracking policy the difference is what scales in. My first idea breaks because forecast only mode does not scale the group at all, in either direction, and predictive scaling does not scale in. So the group needs a dynamic policy, and target tracking follows the load, which costs less than a fixed evening action.
Check: target tracking plus the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready and removes capacity at night. Time: 90 seconds.
